goals: Explain why a prism splits white light and why violet deviates most and red least
List the colours of the visible spectrum in order of wavelength
Arrange the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength

slides.heading: Where do the colours come from?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — sunlight looks white, yet a glass prism, a cut-glass chandelier or a soap bubble shows it is a mixture of colours. And visible light is only a tiny part of a much bigger family of waves.

rows: Colours from a chandelier drop in sunlight
White light is a mixture of colours
A prism spreads a beam into a band
Each colour bends by a different amount
A TV remote works without visible light
There is radiation our eyes cannot see

visual.alt: Table of four observations and what each shows about light and radiation

slides.narration: Namaste! Hang a cut glass drop in a sunny window and you will see patches of colour on the wall. White sunlight is really a mixture of colours, and glass can separate them. In this part we see how a prism does this, and we meet the whole family of electromagnetic waves, of which visible light is only a small part.

slides.heading: Dispersion of white light by a prism
slides.body_md: When a narrow beam of white light passes through a glass prism, it splits into a band of colours called a **spectrum**: **V I B G Y O R** — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. This splitting is **dispersion**. **Red** is deviated **least** (it appears nearest the apex side) and **violet** is deviated **most** (nearest the base). A prism does not create the colours; it only **separates** colours already present in white light.

slides.narration: Shine a narrow beam of white light through a prism onto a screen and a band of colours appears: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red. This splitting of white light is called dispersion. Red is bent the least and violet the most. The prism does not add colour; it separates the colours that were already mixed in the white light.

slides.heading: Why the colours separate
slides.body_md: In **vacuum (or air)** all colours travel at the same speed, $3 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹. In **glass** each colour has a **different speed**, so the **refractive index of glass depends on the colour (wavelength)**: it is **largest for violet** (shortest wavelength, slowest) and **smallest for red** (longest wavelength, fastest). A larger refractive index means more bending, so **violet deviates most and red least**.

visual.alt: Table of wavelength, refractive index of crown glass and deviation for four colours

slides.narration: Why are the colours bent by different amounts? In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed. Inside glass, violet light travels a little more slowly than red light. So glass has a slightly higher refractive index for violet than for red. A higher refractive index means more bending, so violet is deviated the most and red the least.

slides.heading: Worked example: red and violet in glass
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The refractive index of a crown glass is 1.513 for red light and 1.532 for violet light. Find the speed of each colour in the glass and say which is deviated more by a prism. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹)

**Red:** $v = \dfrac{c}{\mu} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.513} = 1.98 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹.

**Violet:** $v = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.532} = 1.96 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹.

Violet is slower in glass (larger $\mu$), so it is **deviated more**.

visual.alt: Table of refractive index and speed of red and violet light in crown glass

slides.narration: Divide the speed of light in air by each refractive index. Red light travels at about one point nine eight times ten to the eight metres per second in the glass, and violet at about one point nine six. The difference is small, but violet is slower, has the larger refractive index, and so is bent more by the prism.

slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that violet has the largest refractive index in glass.

slides.heading: The visible spectrum
slides.body_md: The **visible spectrum** stretches from about **400 nm (violet)** to about **700–800 nm (red)** (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m). In order of **increasing wavelength**: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. Since $c = f \lambda$, the order of **increasing frequency** is the reverse. Light of a **single wavelength** (for example from a sodium lamp) is **monochromatic** and is **not** split by a prism.

slides.narration: The visible spectrum runs from violet, with a wavelength of about four hundred nanometres, to red, at about seven hundred to eight hundred nanometres. Violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency; red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency. Light of one single wavelength, such as the yellow of a sodium lamp, cannot be split any further.

slides.heading: Worked example: frequencies of violet and red
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the frequencies of violet light ($\lambda = 400$ nm) and red light ($\lambda = 700$ nm) in air. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹)

**Violet:** $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{4.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 7.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

**Red:** $f = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{7.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.29 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

Violet has the **higher** frequency; red the **lower**.

visual.alt: Table of wavelength and frequency of violet and red light

slides.narration: Frequency equals the speed of light divided by wavelength. For violet light of four hundred nanometres, that gives seven and a half times ten to the fourteen hertz. For red light of seven hundred nanometres, it is about four point three times ten to the fourteen hertz. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency.

slides.narration: Quick check. Red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.

slides.heading: The electromagnetic spectrum
slides.body_md:
Visible light is one small band of a continuous family of **electromagnetic (EM) waves**. In order of **increasing wavelength** (decreasing frequency):

**gamma rays → X-rays → ultraviolet → visible → infrared → microwaves → radio waves**

Approximate wavelengths: gamma below 10⁻¹¹ m; X-rays 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁸ m; UV 10⁻⁸ m to 4 × 10⁻⁷ m; visible 4 × 10⁻⁷ to 8 × 10⁻⁷ m; infrared 8 × 10⁻⁷ m to 10⁻³ m; microwaves 10⁻³ to about 0.3 m; radio waves longer.

slides.narration: Visible light belongs to a much larger family called the electromagnetic spectrum. Arranged from the shortest wavelength to the longest, the family is gamma rays, X rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves and radio waves. On this scale each step is a factor of one hundred, and the visible band is a narrow sliver.

slides.heading: Properties common to all EM waves

rows: Deflected by electric or magnetic fields?

visual.alt: Table of five properties shared by all electromagnetic waves

slides.narration: Although they behave very differently, all electromagnetic waves have a lot in common. They are made of changing electric and magnetic fields at right angles. They are transverse waves that can travel through empty space, all at three hundred thousand kilometres per second. They are not bent by electric or magnetic fields, and they can be reflected and refracted.

slides.heading: Worked example: which region is it?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Identify the region of each radiation. (a) A Wi-Fi router transmits at $6.0 \times 10^{9}$ Hz. (b) A heat lamp emits most strongly at $\lambda = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m. ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹)

**(a)** $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{6.0 \times 10^{9}} = 0.05$ m $= 5$ cm: between $10^{-3}$ m and 0.3 m, so **microwaves**.

**(b)** $2.0 \times 10^{-6}$ m lies between $8 \times 10^{-7}$ m and $10^{-3}$ m: **infrared**. Its frequency is $\dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{2.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz.

visual.alt: Table identifying the region of the Wi-Fi signal and the heat lamp radiation

slides.narration: To place a radiation in the spectrum, find its wavelength. For the Wi Fi signal, wavelength is speed divided by frequency, which gives five centimetres: that is in the microwave region. The heat lamp’s wavelength of two micrometres is longer than red light but much shorter than a millimetre, so it is infrared.

slides.heading: Quick check: a wavelength from a frequency
slides.body_md: Use c = f λ to find a wavelength.
slides.narration: Quick check. Wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Dispersion: splitting of white light into VIBGYOR by a prism.
Cause: refractive index of glass depends on colour; largest for violet, smallest for red.
Violet deviated most, red least; in vacuum all colours have the same speed.
EM spectrum by increasing wavelength: gamma, X-rays, UV, visible, IR, microwaves, radio.
All EM waves: transverse, travel through vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, c = f λ, not deflected by fields.

visual.alt: Summary table of four key facts from Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. A prism splits white light because glass has a different refractive index for each colour, so violet bends most and red least. Visible light is one small band in the electromagnetic spectrum, which runs from gamma rays to radio waves. All these waves are transverse and travel through vacuum at the same speed.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Say the prism SEPARATES colours already in white light; it does not produce them.
Link: shorter wavelength → larger μ in glass → more deviation.
Memorise the EM order with wavelengths: gamma, X, UV, visible, IR, micro, radio.
In c = f λ, convert nm to m (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m) and GHz to Hz.

rows: Speed of colours differs in vacuum

slides.narration: Some tips. Write that a prism separates the colours already present in white light. Explain dispersion with the chain: shorter wavelength, larger refractive index, more bending. Learn the order of the electromagnetic spectrum. And in calculations, change nanometres to metres and gigahertz to hertz before using the wave equation.

slides.heading: Light beyond red and violet
slides.body_md: Part 2 — just beyond the red end of the spectrum lies **infrared**, which we feel as heat; just beyond the violet end lies **ultraviolet**, which tans skin. And the way air scatters sunlight paints the sky blue.

rows: Warmth felt near a heater or a hot tawa
Sun tan after a day at the beach

visual.alt: Table of radiations and effects with everyday examples

slides.narration: Stand near a hot tawa and you feel its warmth without touching it; that is infrared radiation. Spend a day in strong sunshine and your skin may tan; that is ultraviolet. Neither can be seen. In this part we study these two invisible radiations, and then find out why the sky is blue.

slides.heading: Infrared radiation: production, detection and properties
slides.body_md:
**Infrared (IR)** lies beyond the red end of the visible spectrum ($8 \times 10^{-7}$ m to $10^{-3}$ m). It was found by placing a thermometer beyond the red end of a solar spectrum: the temperature rose.
- **Produced** by all hot bodies: the Sun, a heater coil, a hot iron, our bodies.
- **Detected** by its **heating effect**: a thermometer with a blackened bulb, or a **thermopile**; also by special photographic films and sensors.
- **Properties:** strong **heating effect**; **less scattered** by haze and fog than visible light (longer wavelength); **absorbed by water vapour and carbon dioxide**; mostly **reflected by** shiny surfaces; obeys reflection and refraction.

rows: Heating effect; little scattering by haze

visual.alt: Table of the position, source, detector and key property of infrared radiation

slides.narration: Infrared lies just beyond red light. Every hot object gives it out, from the Sun to a heater coil to your own body. We detect it by its heating effect, using a blackened thermometer or a thermopile. Because its wavelength is long, it is scattered much less by haze and fog than visible light.

slides.heading: Uses of infrared
slides.body_md:
- **Remote controls** of TVs and air conditioners.
- **Night vision and thermal cameras**, and **photography through haze or fog** (little scattering).
- **Physiotherapy:** IR lamps warm muscles and relieve pain.
- **Drying and heating:** drying paint on cars, cooking, warming rooms; greenhouses trap infrared.
- **Weather forecasting** with infrared photographs from satellites, and **intruder alarms**.

rows: Invisible signal, easily detected by a sensor
Warm bodies give out more infrared

visual.alt: Table of four uses of infrared radiation and the property each uses

slides.narration: Infrared has many uses. Your television remote sends invisible infrared pulses. Thermal cameras see warm bodies in the dark. Pictures taken with infrared cut through haze. Doctors use infrared lamps to warm aching muscles, and factories use them to dry paint. Weather satellites take infrared photographs of clouds.

slides.heading: Worked example: radiation from a heater
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The element of a room heater emits radiation most strongly at a wavelength of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ m. (a) Find its frequency. (b) Name the region. (c) Why do you feel it as warmth but cannot see it? ($c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹)

**(a)** $f = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 2.0 \times 10^{13}$ Hz.

**(b)** The wavelength is longer than $8 \times 10^{-7}$ m and shorter than $10^{-3}$ m: **infrared**.

**(c)** Infrared has a strong heating effect, but its wavelength is beyond the range the eye can detect.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the heater example

slides.narration: Frequency is the speed of light divided by wavelength, which gives two times ten to the thirteen hertz. The wavelength is longer than red light but shorter than a millimetre, so this is infrared. You feel it because infrared has a strong heating effect, but your eyes cannot detect wavelengths that long.

slides.body_md: Identify the radiation beyond the red end of a spectrum.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which radiation has a strong heating effect.

slides.heading: Ultraviolet radiation: production, detection and properties
slides.body_md:
**Ultraviolet (UV)** lies beyond the violet end ($10^{-8}$ m to $4 \times 10^{-7}$ m).
- **Produced** by very hot bodies such as the **Sun**, electric **arcs** (welding), and **mercury vapour lamps** in quartz tubes.
- **Detected** by **photographic film** and by **fluorescence**: zinc sulphide or fluorescent paint glows when UV falls on it.
- **Properties:** causes **fluorescence**; affects photographic plates; **kills germs**; causes **chemical changes** (tanning, fading of colours); **absorbed by ordinary glass** but passes through **quartz**; mostly **absorbed by the ozone layer**.

rows: Sun, electric arc, mercury vapour lamp

visual.alt: Table of the position, sources, detectors and transmission of ultraviolet radiation

slides.narration: Ultraviolet lies just beyond violet light. The Sun, welding arcs and mercury vapour lamps give it out. We detect it with photographic film, or because it makes certain paints glow. Ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet, so prisms and lamps for it are made of quartz. High in the atmosphere, the ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet.

slides.heading: Uses and dangers of ultraviolet
slides.body_md:
**Uses:** **sterilising** water, surgical instruments and air (kills bacteria); **detecting forged notes** and documents (special inks fluoresce); helping the skin make **vitamin D**; fluorescent tubes; studying molecular structure.

**Dangers:** too much UV causes **sunburn**, damages the **eyes** and can cause **skin cancer**. Welders wear dark goggles; we use sunscreen. The **ozone layer** protects life by absorbing most solar UV.

visual.alt: Table of uses and dangers of ultraviolet radiation and the property behind each

slides.narration: Ultraviolet kills germs, so it is used to purify water and sterilise instruments. Bank staff check notes under ultraviolet lamps, because special inks glow. A little ultraviolet helps our skin make vitamin D, but too much burns the skin and harms the eyes. That is why welders wear dark goggles and why the ozone layer matters.

slides.heading: Scattering of light
slides.body_md: When light falls on very small particles (air molecules, fine dust), the particles absorb it and send it out again in **all directions**. This is **scattering**. For particles much **smaller than the wavelength**, the intensity of scattered light is roughly proportional to $\dfrac{1}{\lambda^{4}}$ (Rayleigh’s law). So **shorter wavelengths (violet, blue)** are scattered **much more** than **longer wavelengths (red)**. Large particles (water droplets in clouds) scatter all colours **almost equally**.

visual.alt: Graph of relative scattering against wavelength, falling steeply from one at four hundred nanometres to about one tenth at seven hundred nanometres
visual.caption: Shorter wavelengths are scattered far more strongly.

slides.narration: Tiny particles such as air molecules take in light and send it out again in all directions. This is scattering. It depends strongly on wavelength: halve the wavelength and the scattering becomes sixteen times stronger. So violet and blue light are scattered far more than red. Big water droplets, however, scatter all colours about equally.

slides.heading: Worked example: blue against red
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Compare the scattering of blue light ($\lambda = 450$ nm) with that of red light ($\lambda = 675$ nm) by air molecules.

**Ratio** $= \left(\dfrac{\lambda_{red}}{\lambda_{blue}}\right)^{4} = \left(\dfrac{675}{450}\right)^{4} = 1.5^{4} = 5.0625$.

So blue light is scattered about **5 times** as strongly as red light. This is why scattered skylight looks blue.

visual.alt: Table of wavelength and relative scattering for blue and red light

slides.narration: Scattering goes as one over the fourth power of wavelength, so the ratio is the red wavelength over the blue wavelength, raised to the fourth power. Six hundred and seventy five divided by four hundred and fifty is one and a half, and one and a half to the fourth power is about five. Blue is scattered about five times as strongly as red.

slides.heading: Blue sky and red sunrise
slides.body_md:
**Blue sky:** sunlight crossing the atmosphere is scattered by air molecules; **blue** (and violet) is scattered most, so light reaching us from all parts of the sky is mainly blue. (Our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some violet is absorbed high up, so the sky looks blue rather than violet.)

**Red Sun at sunrise and sunset:** the Sun is near the horizon, so its light travels a **much longer path** through the air. Most of the blue is scattered out of the beam on the way, and the light that reaches us is mainly **red and orange**. At noon the path is short, so the Sun looks white.

slides.narration: At noon, sunlight crosses only a short thickness of air, and the Sun looks white. The blue light scattered sideways fills the sky. At sunrise, the Sun is on the horizon and its light must cross a much longer path through the air. By the time it reaches you, most of the blue has been scattered away, so the Sun looks red.

slides.heading: Other effects of scattering
slides.body_md:
- **Danger signals and brake lights are red:** red is scattered **least**, so it travels farthest through fog and smoke and is seen from a distance.
- **Clouds are white:** water droplets are large compared with the wavelength and scatter **all colours** about equally.
- **The sky looks black** from the Moon or to an astronaut in space: there is **no air** to scatter sunlight.
- **The deep sea looks blue**, partly because of scattering of blue light by water and partly by reflection of the sky.

slides.narration: Scattering explains more everyday sights. Danger signals are red because red light is scattered least and can be seen from far away, even in mist. Clouds look white because their big water drops scatter all colours equally. And on the Moon, which has no air, the sky is black even when the Sun is shining.

notes.title: Spectrum — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Dispersion of white light
sections.body_md:
- **Dispersion:** the splitting of white light into its constituent colours by a prism. The band of colours is the **spectrum**: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR).
- **Cause:** in a material medium, light of different colours travels at different speeds, so the **refractive index depends on wavelength**: $\mu_{violet} > \mu_{red}$. Hence **violet is deviated most and red least**.
- In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed, $3 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹.
- A prism only separates colours already present; a second, identical prism placed inverted recombines them into white light.
- **Monochromatic light** (one wavelength, for example a sodium lamp) is deviated but not dispersed.

key_terms.definition_md: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours on passing through a prism.
The band of colours obtained when white light is dispersed.
Light of a single wavelength (single colour).

visual.alt: Table comparing red and violet light in glass

sections.heading: 2. The visible spectrum
sections.body_md:
- Wavelength range about **400 nm (violet) to 700–800 nm (red)**; $1\ \text{nm} = 10^{-9}$ m.
- Order of increasing wavelength: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red; frequency increases the other way ($c = f\lambda$).
- Colour is decided by **frequency**, which does not change on refraction.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance between two successive crests (or compressions) of a wave.

visual.alt: Table of wavelength and frequency of violet, green and red light

sections.heading: 3. The electromagnetic spectrum
sections.body_md:
| Region | Wavelength (about) | Source or use |
|---|---|---|
| Gamma rays | below 10⁻¹¹ m | Radioactive nuclei; cancer treatment |
| X-rays | 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻⁸ m | Fast electrons hitting a metal; bone images |
| Ultraviolet | 10⁻⁸ to 4 × 10⁻⁷ m | Sun, arcs; sterilising |
| Visible | 4 × 10⁻⁷ to 8 × 10⁻⁷ m | Sun, lamps; seeing |
| Infrared | 8 × 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻³ m | Hot bodies; remote controls |
| Microwaves | 10⁻³ to 0.3 m | Ovens, radar, mobile phones |
| Radio waves | above 0.3 m | Broadcasting |

**Common properties:** produced by accelerated charges; transverse electric and magnetic fields; travel in vacuum at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹; obey $c = f\lambda$; not deflected by electric or magnetic fields; can be reflected and refracted; carry energy.

key_terms.definition_md: A transverse wave of changing electric and magnetic fields that can travel through vacuum at the speed of light.

visual.alt: Table showing the two ends of the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.heading: 4. Infrared and ultraviolet radiation
sections.body_md:
**Infrared (IR):** beyond red. Produced by hot bodies (Sun, heater, human body). Detected by a thermopile or blackened-bulb thermometer. Properties: strong heating effect; less scattered by haze and fog; absorbed by water vapour and CO₂; reflected by polished surfaces. Uses: remote controls, night vision and thermal cameras, haze photography, physiotherapy, drying paint, weather satellites, greenhouses.

**Ultraviolet (UV):** beyond violet. Produced by the Sun, electric arcs, mercury vapour lamps (quartz tubes). Detected by photographic film and fluorescence (zinc sulphide). Properties: causes fluorescence; kills germs; causes chemical changes (tanning); absorbed by ordinary glass, transmitted by quartz; absorbed by the ozone layer. Uses: sterilising water and instruments, checking forged notes, vitamin D formation. Harmful in excess: sunburn, eye damage, skin cancer.

key_terms.definition_md: A detector of infrared radiation that produces a current when warmed by the radiation.
The emission of visible light by a substance while ultraviolet radiation falls on it.

visual.alt: Table comparing infrared and ultraviolet radiation

sections.heading: 5. Scattering of light
sections.body_md:
- **Scattering:** absorption and re-emission of light in all directions by small particles.
- For particles much smaller than the wavelength (air molecules): scattered intensity $\propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda^{4}}$. Blue is scattered about 5 times as much as red.
- **Blue sky:** air molecules scatter blue most; skylight is mainly blue.
- **Red Sun at sunrise and sunset:** long path through air removes blue by scattering; red reaches the eye.
- **Red danger signals:** red is scattered least and penetrates fog farthest.
- **White clouds:** large droplets scatter all colours equally.
- **Black sky in space or on the Moon:** no atmosphere, no scattering.

key_terms.definition_md: The process by which small particles absorb light and send it out again in all directions.

rows: Blue scattered out on a long path

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying red is deviated (or scattered) most.
- Saying the prism “produces” colours.
- Mixing up the order of the electromagnetic spectrum, especially X-rays and gamma rays, or infrared and microwaves.
- Forgetting that ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet.
- Explaining the red sunrise without mentioning the longer path through air.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Dispersion: definition (1), cause — μ depends on wavelength (1), order of deviation (1).
- IR and UV: each property or use 1 mark; a named detector or source earns credit.
- Scattering: name the particles, the wavelength dependence and the conclusion.

questions.stem_md: The refractive index of a crown glass for violet light is 1.532. Find the speed of violet light in this glass, in units of 10⁸ m/s, to three significant figures.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a glass prism splits white light into colours, while a single colour such as pure red light is only bent, not split.

answer.model_answer_md: White light is a mixture of colours, and glass has a different refractive index for each colour (largest for violet, smallest for red), so each colour is bent through a different angle and they separate. questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by dispersion of light? State its cause. [3]

(b) Describe, as you would draw it, the passage of a narrow beam of white light through a glass prism onto a screen. Which colour is deviated (i) the most and (ii) the least? [3]

(c) (i) Yellow light has a refractive index of 1.62 in a flint glass. Find its speed in the glass. (ii) Is the refractive index of this glass for blue light more or less than 1.62? (iii) How can the spectrum be recombined into white light? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its constituent colours when it passes through a prism. Cause: the refractive index of glass is different for different colours (wavelengths), so each colour is deviated by a different amount.

(b) The beam bends towards the base at both faces and spreads into a band of colours, VIBGYOR, with red nearest the apex side and violet nearest the base. (i) Violet. (ii) Red.

(c) (i) $v = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.62} = 1.85 \times 10^{8}$ m/s. (ii) More: blue has a shorter wavelength than yellow. (iii) Place a second identical prism, inverted, close to the first; it reverses the deviations and the colours mix to white.

questions.solution_md: Definition and cause; diagram; speed and recombination.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is scattering of light? How does the intensity of scattered light depend on wavelength, for very small particles? [3]

(b) Explain (i) why the clear sky looks blue and (ii) why the Sun looks red at sunrise. [3]

(c) (i) How many times more strongly is light of wavelength 400 nm scattered than light of 600 nm? (ii) Why are clouds white? (iii) Why is the sky black for an astronaut in space? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Scattering is the absorption of light by small particles and its re-emission in all directions. For particles much smaller than the wavelength, the intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength.

(b) (i) Air molecules scatter short wavelengths (blue) much more than long ones, so light reaching us from all over the sky is mainly blue. (ii) At sunrise sunlight travels a long path through the air; blue is scattered out on the way and mainly red reaches the eye.

(c) (i) $\left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{4} = 1.5^{4} = 5.063$, about 5 times. (ii) Cloud droplets are large compared with the wavelength and scatter all colours about equally. (iii) There is no air in space to scatter sunlight towards the eye.

questions.solution_md: Definition and law; blue sky and red sunrise; ratio and two effects.

questions.stem_md:
Sunlight is passed through a quartz prism to form a spectrum on a long white card. A thermometer with a blackened bulb and a strip of fluorescent paper are moved along the card, well beyond both ends of the visible band.

(a) Where does the thermometer show the greatest rise in temperature? Name the radiation and explain your answer. [3]

(b) Where does the fluorescent paper glow? Name the radiation. Why is a quartz prism used instead of glass? [3]

(c) (i) Radiation at point A has a wavelength of 900 nm and at point B of 300 nm. Find their frequencies. (ii) Which point lies beyond the red end? (iii) Predict what happens to the glow at B if a sheet of window glass is held in front of the card. (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Just beyond the red end: infrared radiation falls there, and infrared has a strong heating effect, which the blackened bulb absorbs.

(b) Just beyond the violet end: ultraviolet radiation, which causes fluorescence. Ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet, but quartz transmits it, so with a glass prism the ultraviolet would not reach the card.

(c) (i) $f_{A} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{9.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.33 \times 10^{14}$ Hz; $f_{B} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{3.0 \times 10^{-7}} = 1.0 \times 10^{15}$ Hz. (ii) A (900 nm, longer than red). (iii) The glow fades or stops, because the glass absorbs the ultraviolet.

questions.solution_md: Infrared region; ultraviolet region and quartz; frequencies and prediction.
